perspective:
From Sara Manuelito’s perspective, she has access to the following:

- I know Shirley Whiteplume as a nurse, long-time colleague, and close friend from our years working together at the community health center.
- I attended the funeral of our mutual patient. I saw Shirley there and noticed she seemed somber; I suspected she was deeply affected by the loss.
- At the funeral, I told Shirley I knew it must be hard and that I saw how much she cared. Shirley told me it had been tough, that she kept thinking whether more could have been done, and that it was hard to let go. I told her we did everything we could and should remember the good care and joy we brought him.
- During a coffee break at work, I brought up our treatment decisions and said I sensed she felt burdened. Shirley told me she felt responsible, wondered if pushing for a different approach might have helped, and said it was hard to accept. I told her we made the best decisions with the information we had.
- I observed Shirley continuing to be reserved and minimally expressive. In a quiet moment in our office, I told her I noticed she was holding back feelings and that it is okay to be open. Shirley told me she did not want to seem unprofessional or weak, and later said she would try to be more open.
- I later felt my previous confrontation might have been too harsh, so I apologized to Shirley for coming on too strong. Shirley told me it was a bit much but that she knew I meant well, appreciated the apology, and wanted us to keep talking because it helps.
- After some time, I noticed Shirley seemed to be doing better. I asked how she was feeling. Shirley told me she was feeling better thanks to our talks and my support. I suggested spending more time together outside work, and Shirley agreed to plan something for the weekend.

I do not have access to Shirley’s private, unspoken thoughts or any events I did not observe or hear about directly.
